results.title: Glauberman's $Z^*$-theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Glauberman's $Z^*$-theorem. Let $G$ be a finite group and let $t \in G$ be an involution ($t \neq 1$ and $t^2 = 1$) such that every conjugate $g t g^{-1}$ of $t$ that commutes with $t$ equals $t$. Then there is a normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ of odd order such that $g t g^{-1} t^{-1} \in N$ for every $g \in G$.

results.title: Odd core from normal subgroups of odd-order elements
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a group $G$, $O(G)$ is the join, in the lattice of subgroups of $G$, of all normal subgroups $N$ of $G$ such that every element of $N$ has finite odd order. In a periodic group this join is again a normal subgroup consisting of elements of odd order, so it is the largest such subgroup.

results.title: Borovik's question on involutions with odd-order products (Kourovka 11.13)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a group $G$, let $O(G)$ be the join of all normal subgroups of $G$ all of whose elements have odd order. This is the statement that for every periodic group $G$ and every involution $i \in G$ such that $g^{-1} i g i$ has odd order for every $g \in G$, the image of $i$ in $G / O(G)$ is central, that is, $g i g^{-1} i^{-1} \in O(G)$ for every $g \in G$.

results.title: A periodic counterexample to Borovik's question (Kourovka 11.13)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a group $G$, let $O(G)$ be the join of all normal subgroups of $G$ all of whose elements have odd order. There exist a periodic group $G$ and an involution $i \in G$ such that $g^{-1} i g i$ has odd order for every $g \in G$, but the image of $i$ in $G / O(G)$ is not central: $g i g^{-1} i^{-1} \notin O(G)$ for some $g \in G$. This answers Kourovka Problem 11.13 in the negative.

results.title: Normal subgroups of exponent p in p-groups when p > n

results.title: Truncated logarithmic polynomial
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, the truncated logarithmic polynomial is $F_n(x) = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2} + \dots + \frac{x^n}{n} \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$.

results.title: Least common multiple of $1, \dots, n$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, $L_n$ is the least common multiple $\operatorname{lcm}(1, 2, \dots, n)$ of the integers from $1$ to $n$; in particular $L_0 = 1$.

results.title: Least common multiple of $1, 2, 3, 4$

results.title: Scaled truncated logarithmic polynomial

results.title: The scaled truncated logarithmic polynomial is $L_n F_n$

Mapping the coefficients of $\tilde F_n$ from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ gives the polynomial $L_n F_n$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.

results.title: Scaled factorial product at index zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ of natural numbers, $\prod_{a \in L} (a \cdot 0)! = 1$, since every factor equals $0! = 1$.

results.title: Scaled factorial products at index zero divide
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all lists $A$ and $B$ of natural numbers, $\prod_{b \in B} (b \cdot 0)!$ divides $\prod_{a \in A} (a \cdot 0)!$, since both products equal $1$.

results.title: Characterization of integral factorial ratios

results.title: Permuting the numerator of an integral factorial ratio

results.title: Permuting the denominator of an integral factorial ratio

results.title: Integral factorial ratios are invariant under permutation

results.title: Equal singletons form an integral factorial ratio

results.title: The central binomial factorial ratio is integral

results.title: Sloane's endpoint formula for reverse multiples
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g$ and $k$ be integers with $2 \le k < g$, and let $N = (a_n a_{n-1} \cdots a_0)_g$ have base-$g$ digits $a_0, \dots, a_n \in \{0, \dots, g - 1\}$, with units digit $a_0$ and leading digit $a_n \ne 0$. Suppose $N$ is a $(g, k)$ reverse multiple, that is, $k N = (a_0 a_1 \cdots a_n)_g$, and that $a_0 + a_n = g$. Then $(k + 1) a_n = g$; in particular $k + 1$ divides $g$ and $a_n = g / (k + 1)$.

results.title: Sutcliffe's theorem on two- and three-digit reverse multiples
results.caption: Theorem

Then $a + b < g$, so $a + b$ is a base-$g$ digit, and $(a\,(a + b)\,b)_g$ is again a $(g, k)$ reverse multiple, that is, $k (a g^2 + (a + b) g + b) = b g^2 + (a + b) g + a$.

results.title: Multigraph
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A multigraph on a vertex set $V$ is given by an edge multiplicity function $m$ that assigns to every two vertices $v, w \in V$ a natural number $m(v, w)$ and is symmetric: $m(v, w) = m(w, v)$ for all $v, w \in V$. Loops are permitted: $m(v, v)$ may be positive.

results.title: Adjacency in a multigraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two vertices $v$ and $w$ of a multigraph $G$ are adjacent when the edge multiplicity between $v$ and $w$ is positive.

results.title: Degree of a vertex in a multigraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a multigraph $G$ on a finite vertex set $V$ with edge multiplicity $m$, the degree of a vertex $v$ is $\sum_{w \in V} m(v, w)$. A loop at $v$ contributes its multiplicity once, matching the outgoing-isogeny convention.

results.title: Degree restricted to a predicate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a multigraph on a finite vertex set $V$ with edge multiplicity $m$, let $v \in V$ and let $P$ be a decidable predicate on $V$. The degree of $v$ restricted to $P$ is $\sum_{w \in V,\, P(w)} m(v, w)$.

results.title: Connectivity of vertices in a multigraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two vertices $v$ and $w$ of a multigraph $G$ are connected when they are related by the reflexive-transitive closure of adjacency, that is, when there is a finite sequence of vertices $v = u_0, u_1, \dots, u_k = w$ with $k \ge 0$ and $u_i$ adjacent to $u_{i+1}$ for each $i < k$.

results.title: Connected multigraph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A multigraph $G$ is connected when every two vertices $v$ and $w$ of $G$ are joined by a walk, that is, $w$ is reachable from $v$ by a finite (possibly empty) sequence of steps along edges of positive multiplicity.

results.title: Symmetry of adjacency in a multigraph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a multigraph $G$, a vertex $v$ is adjacent to a vertex $w$ if and only if $w$ is adjacent to $v$.

results.title: Every vertex is connected to itself
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a multigraph $G$, every vertex $v$ is connected to $v$.

results.title: Degree splits over a predicate and its complement
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a multigraph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $v \in V$ and let $P$ be a decidable predicate on $V$. Then the degree of $v$ equals the degree of $v$ restricted to $P$ plus the degree of $v$ restricted to $\neg P$.

results.title: Restricted degree depends only on the neighbours
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a multigraph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $v \in V$ and let $P$ and $Q$ be decidable predicates on $V$. If $P(w) \iff Q(w)$ for every vertex $w$ whose edge multiplicity with $v$ is positive, then the degree of $v$ restricted to $P$ equals the degree of $v$ restricted to $Q$.

results.title: Surface of a volcano
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A vertex $v$ of an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$ lies on the surface of $C$ when its level is $0$.

results.title: Floor of a volcano
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A vertex $v$ of an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$ of depth $d$ lies on the floor of $C$ when its level is $d$, the last of the levels $0, 1, \dots, d$.

results.title: Depth of an isogeny volcano
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The depth of an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$ is the natural number $d$ recorded in $C$: the levels of the vertices of $C$ are exactly $0, 1, \dots, d$, with level $0$ the surface and level $d$ the floor.

results.title: Horizontal edge
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$, the pair $(v, w)$ of vertices is a horizontal edge when the edge multiplicity between $v$ and $w$ is positive and both $v$ and $w$ lie on the surface, that is, both have level $0$.

results.title: Descending edge
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$, the pair $(v, w)$ of vertices is a descending edge when the edge multiplicity between $v$ and $w$ is positive and $w$ lies one level below $v$, that is, the level of $v$ plus one equals the level of $w$ (level $0$ being the surface).

results.title: Ascending edge
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$, the pair $(v, w)$ of vertices is an ascending edge when the edge multiplicity between $v$ and $w$ is positive and $w$ lies one level above $v$, that is, the level of $w$ plus one equals the level of $v$ (level $0$ being the surface).

results.title: Vertical edge
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$, the pair $(v, w)$ of vertices is a vertical edge when it is a descending edge or an ascending edge, that is, when the edge multiplicity between $v$ and $w$ is positive and the levels of $v$ and $w$ differ by exactly one.

results.title: Reversing a descending edge gives an ascending edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In an $\ell$-isogeny volcano, for vertices $v$ and $w$, $(v, w)$ is a descending edge if and only if $(w, v)$ is an ascending edge.

results.title: Reversing an ascending edge gives a descending edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In an $\ell$-isogeny volcano, for vertices $v$ and $w$, $(v, w)$ is an ascending edge if and only if $(w, v)$ is a descending edge.

results.title: Every edge of an isogeny volcano is horizontal, descending or ascending
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C$ be an $\ell$-isogeny volcano, with levels numbered from $0$ at the surface, and let $v, w$ be vertices of $C$ whose edge multiplicity is positive. Then $(v, w)$ is a horizontal edge (both $v$ and $w$ have level $0$), a descending edge (the level of $w$ is the level of $v$ plus one) or an ascending edge (the level of $v$ is the level of $w$ plus one).

results.title: Surface vertices are those of level zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A vertex $v$ of an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$ lies on the surface of $C$ if and only if the level of $v$, as a natural number, is $0$.

results.title: Floor vertices are those whose level equals the depth
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A vertex $v$ of an $\ell$-isogeny volcano $C$ lies on the floor of $C$ if and only if the level of $v$, as a natural number, equals the depth of $C$.

results.title: Surface regularity of an isogeny volcano
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C$ be an $\ell$-isogeny volcano with edge multiplicities $m$ and surface degree $s$. For every surface vertex $v$ of $C$, that is, every vertex of level $0$, the sum of $m(v, w)$ over all surface vertices $w$ of $C$ equals $s$.

results.title: Max-rook number of a board

results.summary: For a finite board $B \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, whose cell $(i, j)$ lies in row $i$ and column $j$, the max-rook number of $B$ is the largest size of a subset of $B$ that contains at most one cell of each row and at most one cell of each column, that is, the largest number of non-attacking rooks that can be placed on $B$.

results.title: Ferrers board of a partition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a partition of $n$, and number rows and columns from $0$. The Ferrers board of $p$ is the finite set of cells $(i, j) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ such that the $(i+1)$-st largest part of $p$ exceeds $j$, that is, such that more than $i$ parts of $p$, counted with multiplicity, exceed $j$.

results.title: Max-rook number of a partition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The max-rook number $R(\pi)$ of a partition $\pi$ of $n$ is the largest number of non-attacking rooks on the Ferrers board of $\pi$: the largest number of cells of the board, no two in the same row and no two in the same column.

results.title: Partitions with a given max-rook number
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $n$, $R_k(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$ whose max-rook number, the largest number of non-attacking rooks on the Ferrers board, equals $k$.

results.title: Largest max-rook number among partitions of $n$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n \ge 1$, $F(n)$ is the largest max-rook number $R(\pi)$ over all partitions $\pi$ of $n$, where $R(\pi)$ is the largest number of non-attacking rooks on the Ferrers board of $\pi$. By convention $F(0) = 1$.

results.title: Incident-edge sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$, let $q$ be a natural number and let $\ell$ be a bijection from the edge set of $G$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}$. The incident-edge sum at a vertex $v$ is $\sum_{e \ni v} (\ell(e) + 1)$, the sum over the edges $e$ of $G$ that contain $v$; in other words, the edges carry the labels $1, \dots, q$.

results.title: Induced vertex residue
results.caption: Definition

The induced residue of a vertex $v$ is the incident-edge sum at $v$ (with edge labels $\ell(e) + 1$) reduced modulo $|V|$, viewed as an element of $\{0, \dots, |V| - 1\}$. When $|V| = 0$ there are no vertices, so there is nothing to define.

results.title: Erasing a key from a list of entries
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a key $k$ and a list of key–value pairs, erasing $k$ deletes every pair whose key is $k$ and keeps the other pairs in their original order. When the keys in the list are pairwise distinct, at most one pair is deleted.

results.title: Empty LRU cache
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every capacity $c$, the empty LRU cache of capacity $c$ is the cache with no entries.

results.title: Key list of an LRU cache
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The key list of an LRU cache is the list of the keys of its entries in the order of the cache, so the most recently used key comes first.

results.title: Size of an LRU cache
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The size of an LRU cache is the number of entries it stores.

results.title: LRU cache lookup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Looking up a key $k$ in an LRU cache returns an optional value together with a cache. If the cache stores a binding $(k, v)$, the result is $v$ together with the cache in which that binding is moved to the front and the other entries keep their order; otherwise the result is no value together with the unchanged cache.

results.title: Insertion into an LRU cache
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Putting the binding $(k, v)$ into an LRU cache of capacity $c$ removes any entry with key $k$, places $(k, v)$ at the front as the most recently used entry, and then keeps only the first $c$ entries, so the least recently used entries beyond the capacity are evicted.

results.title: Keys of an LRU cache are distinct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The keys stored in any LRU cache are pairwise distinct.

results.title: An LRU cache never exceeds its capacity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every LRU cache of capacity $c$ has size at most $c$.

results.title: A lookup of an absent key misses
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the key $k$ is not stored in an LRU cache, then looking up $k$ returns no value and leaves the cache unchanged.

results.title: A lookup of a stored key returns its value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an LRU cache stores the pair $(k, v)$, then looking up $k$ returns $v$.

results.title: A successful lookup moves the entry to the front
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an LRU cache stores the pair $(k, v)$, then after looking up $k$ the most recently used (first) entry of the cache is $(k, v)$.

results.title: Lookup after insertion into an LRU cache
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache of positive capacity, every key $k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ returns $v$.

results.title: Insertion respects the capacity of an LRU cache
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache $C$ of capacity $c$, key $k$ and value $v$, the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ into $C$ has size at most $c$.

results.title: Insertion keeps the keys of an LRU cache distinct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache $C$, key $k$ and value $v$, the keys of the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ into $C$ are pairwise distinct.

results.title: Lookup respects the capacity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache of capacity $c$ and every key $k$, the cache after looking up $k$ holds at most $c$ entries.

results.title: Lookups keep keys distinct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the keys of the cache obtained by looking up $k$ are pairwise distinct.

results.title: Entries after insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache, key $k$ and value $v$, every key-value pair $p$ stored in the cache after putting the binding $(k, v)$ either equals $(k, v)$, or was stored before and has a key different from $k$.

results.title: Lookup preserves the stored bindings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache and every key $k$, a key-value pair is stored in the cache after looking up $k$ if and only if it was stored in the cache before the lookup.

results.title: A lookup permutes the entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the list of entries of the cache after looking up $k$ is a permutation of the list of entries before.

results.title: Lookup preserves the size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the cache after looking up $k$ holds exactly as many entries as before.

results.title: Insertion without eviction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let an LRU cache of capacity $c$ hold fewer than $c$ entries or already store a binding for the key $k$, and let $v$ be a value. Then a key-value pair $p$ is stored in the cache after putting the binding $(k, v)$ if and only if $p = (k, v)$, or $p$ was stored before and the key of $p$ differs from $k$.

results.title: With positive capacity, the inserted binding becomes the most recent entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C$ be an LRU cache of positive capacity, $k$ a key and $v$ a value. After the binding $(k, v)$ is put into $C$, the first entry of the resulting cache, its most recently used entry, is $(k, v)$.

results.title: A put without eviction preserves lookups of other keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C$ be an LRU cache of capacity $c$ that holds fewer than $c$ entries or already stores the key $k$. Then for every key $k' \ne k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k'$ in the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ into $C$ returns the same optional value as looking up $k'$ in $C$.

results.title: The evicted key is the least recently used one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C$ be an LRU cache of capacity $c$, let $k'$ be a key not stored in $C$, and let $k$ be a key stored in $C$. If $k$ is no longer stored after putting $k'$ with any value $v$ into $C$, then $C$ held exactly $c$ entries and $k$ is the last key of $C$, that is, the least recently used one.
